header:
Meeting Header:
- Date/Time: 2027-10-11 22:00 UTC
- Duration: 62 minutes
- Attendees: Jamie Park (Redwood AE), Omar Khan (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Redwood CSM); Priya Rao (Hypatia SRE), Miguel Santos (Hypatia CTO), Elliot Wu (Hypatia Procurement), Hannah Lee (Platform Eng)
summary: High-level discovery on reliability expectations: Hypatia cares about contractual SLA language and acceptable degradation modes. Evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private; primary concerns are partial-degradation behavior, MTTR guarantees, data residency, and penalty/credit mechanics for multi-minute outages. Hypatia requested example runbook snippets and a canary rollback policy. Action: Redwood to send pricing + SLA addendum and schedule technical deep-dive.
topics: SLA wording and uptime measurement windows
Graceful degradation vs hard fail (partial responses, degraded models)
Multi-region routing and regional failover choreography
Canary rollouts, automatic rollback and circuit breakers
Data residency, KMS/HSM and audit logs
transcript:
[00:00] Jamie (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:06] Priya (Hypatia SRE): Priya here. Morning to you all.
[00:09] Miguel (Hypatia CTO): Miguel, hi.
[00:11] Elliot (Procurement): Elliot on the line.
[00:14] Omar (Redwood SE): Omar, Redwood SE.
[00:18] Jamie: Perfect. We set aside an hour to go over how you want reliability encoded into the contract and technical fallbacks. We'll cover behavior during partial degradation, multi-region failover, and what we can guarantee with Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private.
[00:35] Priya: Great. To set context: Hypatia runs inference for real-time assistant features, 99.5% of traffic is sub-200 token requests but we have bursts where sequences hit 2k tokens, and during those we saw latency spikes. Our legal team wants firm SLOs and a clear list of allowed degradation behaviors — like returning cached prefixes versus 502s.
[00:58] Jamie: Understood. Quick clarification — when you say "allowed degradation behaviors" do you mean what the application might see (e.g., truncated responses, lower-quality model variant, or explicit errors)?
[01:08] Priya: All of the above. We prefer graceful degradation — return shorter or partial completions rather than hard errors — but legal may require thresholds for when you'd switch to that behavior and when they'd qualify for credits.
[01:21] Omar: Yeah, our platform supports graded fallbacks: 1) prefix/K-V cache hits, 2) model variant fallback (quantized or smaller family), 3) region steering, 4) explicit circuit-breaker error. Those are policy-driven and plumbed into the routing layer.
[01:36] Hannah (Platform Eng): How deterministic is region steering? If a region fails, what's the expected warmup and cold cache penalty?
[01:44] Omar: Good question. For multi-region we keep per-region KV caches if you opt in; warmup depends on your workload shape. For short outages we prefer transparent failover with cached prefixes served while the KV fills. For longer outages, fallback to smaller model variants provides capacity but accuracy degrades. Warmup might cost you increased P95s for a few minutes.
[02:08] Miguel: From a contractual angle, our security/policy folks want MTTR targets and how credits are measured. Is MTTR measured from detection or customer-reported?
[02:18] Jamie: By default our SLA windows measure from when we detect a service-impacting incident in our monitoring and automatically open an incident ticket. But we're flexible in Enterprise agreements; we can add clauses for customer-reported incidents if you need symmetric treatment.
[02:33] Priya: We also wanted specific language about partial degradation. For example, if you return a truncated completion because of a degraded model, does that count as availability or partial availability?
[02:43] Omar: We define availability at the API surface: a non-2xx response counts as outage. Truncated/shortened but 200 responses are still considered available, but we can add a separate quality metric to track meaningful completion rate. Contracts can include a "quality SLI" in addition to availability SLI.
[03:02] Elliot: For procurement we need to see the proposed credit calculation. Flat percent-of-month credit or sliding scale per minute?
[03:10] Jamie: Typical Enterprise SLAs use a sliding credit tied to monthly uptime percentage. For Dedicated customers we can offer tighter SLOs and smaller credit windows; plus options for monetary credits or future bill offsets. We'll include sample language in the SLA addendum.
[03:24] Priya: Can we get example runbook snippets? We want to see the automatic fallback thresholds and the exact circuit-breaker timeouts.
[03:31] Omar: Absolutely. I'll pull a few runbook examples: a canary rollback policy (evaluates error rate and latency deltas), a circuit breaker config (threshold, cool-off, retry jitter), and a region-failover playbook.
[03:45] Miguel: On the hosted vs dedicated question: what's the difference in mean time to failover and support for private network egress?
[03:54] Jamie: Hosted gives fastest onboarding but fallbacks are controlled by Redwood's global routing — good for most use cases. Dedicated provides reserved capacity in your chosen region(s) with richer SLAs and support for private peering. Private (VPC/on-prem) puts the inference plane in your network so you control ND policies, but the initial setup is heavier. MTTR tends to be lower for Dedicated because you have reserved pools and closer support, but Private gives you ultimate control if you have strict residency requirements.
[04:25] Priya: For Dedicated, do we get N+1 across racks within the region? What about AZ failover?
[04:33] Omar: Dedicated is configurable. We can do N+1 in a cluster and distribute across AZs; our standard Dedicated config for enterprise does cross-AZ redundancy. In the SLA we clarify what counts as zonal vs regional outage.
[04:48] Hannah: If we go with Private, will Redwood still provide the control plane for updates and rollout policies or is that fully customer-managed?
[04:56] Jamie: For Private we run a control plane you can opt to host with us or to self-host. Many customers choose a hybrid: control plane in the customer VPC with Redwood-managed runtime images. We can add a clause about maintenance windows so you have predictability.
[05:14] Priya: Back to quality SLI — can you instrument the model family fallbacks and attribute quality loss to fallback events for credits?
[05:23] Omar: Yes, we emit telemetry per-request: which model variant served, whether cache hit, latency, and a quality tag when fallback occurred. We can bake a credit policy that only applies when fallback-induced quality loss exceeded a threshold. That will require mutually agreed telemetry fields and a litmus prompt set for automatic regression detection.
[05:46] Miguel: Our legal team will push for explicit examples where the vendor must use best efforts to route around a failure before crediting. How do you balance aggressive fallback vs trying to maintain higher quality?
[05:57] Jamie: That's where policy tiers come in — you can choose conservative (prefer quality, higher chance of error responses) or permissive (prefer availability, more aggressive fallbacks). We'll map those to pricing tiers.
[06:11] Priya: Can you walk us through a sample incident flow? Say a GPU host in one AZ spikes azure? sorry, spikes CPU causing token generation 10x P95.
[06:23] Omar: Sure. [high level flow]. Detect via p95 anomaly triggers -> traffic automatically routed off the impacted nodes -> traffic routed to healthy nodes in-region -> if region capacity insufficient, routing policy attempts other regions tagged as 'region-failover candidates' -> once cross-region is engaged, KV cache cold-start penalty applies -> after X minutes if error rate still elevated, we spin up fallback model variant. If error persists, circuit breaker trips and we return 503s.
[06:54] Priya: That cold-start penalty — is that typically 30s, a few minutes?
[06:59] Omar: Depends on your prefix hit rates. For typical chat workloads it's often a minute or two for meaningful cache rewarming, but if you have long tails of unique prompts it could be longer. We'll estimate based on your histograms.
[07:11] Miguel: Could we negotiate a clause that for cross-region failover Redwood must attempt warm-warm capacity first (i.e., keep a small buffer in each region) to avoid cold-starts?
[07:21] Jamie: Yes, that's achievable via reserved burst pools or reserved cross-region standby which is optional for Dedicated. It increases cost but reduces warmup pain. We'll put example numbers in the pricing sheet.
[07:34] Priya: On observability: we need token-level breakdown, per-route latency, and model-variant attribution in our logs.
[07:41] Omar: Redwood Console has token-level cost/latency where you can filter by route, model, and time; we can stream those logs into your SIEM and include audit logs for retrievability.
[07:52] Priya: KMS question — for Private, can we integrate with our HSM?
[07:56] Jamie: Yes. For Private we support customer-managed KMS/HSM integrations and bring-your-own-key. We'll provide the integration checklist.
[08:05] Elliot: Procurement side — what about termination for convenience clauses if SLA repeatedly missed? Will there be cure periods?
[08:13] Jamie: Standard practice is cure periods with remediation plans; termination for repeated SLA breaches is negotiable for enterprise deals. We'll include typical legal language and can escalate to legal for redlines.
[08:23] Miguel: We should talk about run rate impact. If we accept a permissive fallback policy that returns lower-quality outputs rather than fail, how will that affect our downstream metric and customer experience?
[08:35] Priya: Right, we don't want to silently degrade experience without telemetry gating.
[08:39] Omar: We recommend a staged approach: Canary in production with a small percent of traffic using the fallback policy and a set of litmus prompts to measure regressions; if quality delta within tolerated band, increase rollout.
[08:50] Jamie: That can be codified into the SLOs too — e.g., a quality SLI measured on the litmus set must remain above X during rollouts, or rollback triggers.
[08:59] Priya: Legal wants explicit time windows for SLA measurement (calendar month vs rolling 30-day). Which do you suggest?
[09:06] Jamie: Most customers pick calendar month for billing alignment, rolling 30-day for operational monitoring. We can propose calendar month for credits.
[09:15] Hannah: Are there constraints for on-prem Private in terms of patch windows? We run a regulated environment and need change freeze windows.
[09:23] Jamie: We can honor maintenance blackout windows and carve them into the contract; for security patches we usually require a narrow window, but can coordinate with your change management.
[09:33] Miguel: Competitors — quick note: we've talked to Vendor X (Anthropic) about model fallbacks and their approach was a single global failover and heavier error rates. Curious about Redwood's multi-tier approach.
[09:45] Omar: Our multi-tier approach provides more control at the routing policy level: you can tune preference for cache, variants, regions, or hard failures. That granularity is a differentiator.
[09:56] Priya: Let's get specific: what does your SLA credit table look like for Dedicated with cross-AZ redundancy?
[10:02] Jamie: Typical example: >=99.9% monthly uptime — no credit; 99.0%-99.9% — 10% credit; 95%-99% — 25% credit; <95% — 50% credit. We'll provide a proposed table and we're open to negotiation. For Private we can adapt language since operations are partly customer-run.
[10:22] Elliot: Are there blackout exclusions for large-scale cloud provider incidents?
[10:27] Jamie: Yes, force majeure and third-party cloud provider incidents are typically called out. We can discuss carving out public cloud provider wide outages vs Redwood-managed infra. For Dedicated with Reserved capacity we can negotiate narrower exclusions.
[10:41] Priya: We need to make sure our SLAs don't create perverse incentives to suppress detection to avoid credits. How do you ensure incident detection and transparency?
[10:52] Omar: We provide incident timelines and postmortems for all incidents affecting customer traffic; for Enterprise we offer direct Slack channels and incident bridge invites. The SLA includes definitions of detection sources and how timelines are recorded.
[11:05] Miguel: Can you support synthetic probing from our side that you will accept as a detection method?
[11:11] Jamie: Yes, we can accept mutually agreed synthetic probes as triggers for the incident timeline. We'll include the specifics: probe endpoints, rate limits, and authentication.
[11:20] Priya: For canary rollbacks, what's the typical criteria? 2x baseline error rate? Latency deltas at P95?
[11:27] Omar: Canary thresholds usually combine error rate delta and latency at P95 over a window. Example: if error rate increases by >1% absolute or P95 latency increases by >200ms vs baseline for 5 continuous minutes, trigger rollback. We can customize.
[11:43] Hannah: If we have a legal dispute on measurement, what is the source of truth?
[11:48] Jamie: We recommend using mutually agreed telemetry exports stored in both parties' systems as the source of truth. That's a common enterprise approach.
[11:57] Miguel: Talk to us about pricing impact of providing warm-standby cross-region capacity. Ballpark numbers?
[12:03] Jamie: We'll put some options: a small cross-region standby (e.g., 10% reserved capacity in a secondary region) typically adds X% to the committed spend. We'll include exact numbers in the pricing sheet.
[12:15] Priya: Is there a way to limit credits to incidents that violate both availability and quality SLIs? We don't want small, brief infra blips to trigger large credits.
[12:25] Omar: Absolutely — you can define a credit trigger that requires breach of both availability and quality SLIs for >Y contiguous minutes. We'll propose sensible defaults.
[12:35] Elliot: From procurement: what documentation do you need to start a PO?
[12:39] Jamie: We'll need your SOW details, estimated committed spend (if Dedicated), legal contact for redlines, and the technical contact for network setup. We'll send a checklist.
[12:50] Priya: One more technical: does Redwood support session affinity for chat flows so KV cache hit rates stay high during failovers?
[12:58] Omar: Yes, session affinity via sticky routing keys is supported; that helps preserve KV cache hits. If you need global affinity across regions, that's a bit trickier but can be approximated with consistent hashing and a small reserved warm pool.
[13:14] Miguel: Good. I think we have the inputs. For next steps, we'll review the SLA draft and reconvene after we review pricing.
[13:22] Jamie: Great. Omar, Lena, we'll prepare the SLA addendum, runbook snippets, and canary configs.
[13:29] Omar: I'll also include an example rollback graph and the actual JSON of the circuit breaker policy so your platform eng can ingest it.
[13:35] Priya: Thanks everyone.
[13:37] Elliot: Thanks.
[13:38] Jamie: Closing notes — we'll aim to send docs by Friday the 15th and book the technical deep-dive for the week of the 18th.
[13:45] Meeting ended.

Notes on transcription quality: occasional misheard acronyms ("K-V cache" sometimes transcribed as "K V cache"), filler words, and overlapping talk in a few places. Some proper nouns may be imperfect.
